questions.stitle: Scenario 1 - City government unifying citizen identity
questions.scenario: You are an Architect in the EA team of a city government building joined-up digital services. The city uses the TOGAF Standard; the Executive Director sponsors the EA program. A Statement of Architecture Work is approved and Phase A is under way. Establishing a single citizen identity is the key challenge because residents currently hold multiple incompatible identities across departments. Two seemingly competing options have emerged: (1) a new digital identity optimized for the flagship service, and (2) a federated model that supports the existing identities across departments. Concerns include fraud, privacy, and the exclusion of residents who lack technology.
questions.q: You have been asked how you would select the best option for the initiative. Which is the best answer?

o.A: Identify the flagship service's stakeholders and their concerns, assess the impact of the two options on the existing departmental IT systems, collaborate with SMEs, assess the security concerns in the Application and Information Systems Architectures, and work with the stakeholders to trade off concerns, changes, costs, and benefits so they select their preferred option.
o.B: Identify the key stakeholders and their concerns, assess the impact of the two options across the architecture domains working with the other domain architects and departmental SMEs, assess the security and privacy concerns in the Business, Application, and Information Systems Architectures, and facilitate the stakeholders selecting their preferred option by trading off concerns, changes, costs, and benefits.
o.C: Identify the stakeholders and the SMEs most involved in information management, assess the impact of the two options on the existing departmental systems, collaborate with the SMEs on the privacy concerns for each option, then select the best option yourself and propose it as the way forward.
o.D: Identify the initiative's stakeholders and departmental leads, work with SMEs to assess the two options using the architecture trade-off method, list the advantages and disadvantages of each, select the best option, integrate it into the Implementation and Migration Plan, explain it to the stakeholders, and oversee its implementation.

rat.B: Best (5). You assess the options across all domains and against multiple concerns so the stakeholders can make a well-informed decision. Security and privacy span uncertainty and defense across every domain, each option reflects one domain's perspective, and only stakeholders decide the relative merit of conflicting concerns.
rat.A: Second (3). It narrows the scope to the flagship service's stakeholders rather than all initiative stakeholders and limits the assessment to the departmental IT systems, ignoring possible Business Architecture impact and part of the security and privacy picture.
rat.C: Third (1). Good EA centers on the stakeholder making an informed decision where interests compete; this is damaged by the architect selecting a best option on unstated criteria and pushing it through. Only stakeholders can approve the Target Architecture.
rat.D: Distractor (0). You are not advising stakeholders across their competing concerns; you are selling a chosen option and stepping into implementation oversight.

questions.scenario: You are an Architect in the EA team of a national restaurant chain launching its own branded food-delivery service instead of relying on third-party apps. The chain uses the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the EA program. An Architecture Vision is approved and there is high-level agreement across domains. A Baseline Description of the current Business Architecture exists, including a business capability map and value stream descriptions for the dine-in business. A packaged delivery-orchestration solution is available but aligns poorly with the current kitchen and point-of-sale systems. The team leader asks how you would identify the changes required in the Business Architecture.

o.A: Determine where the current business (organizational design, processes, capabilities) does not support branded delivery, describe the options for change and their costs to stakeholders so they can decide, identify where trade-off decisions are needed, and work with the stakeholders to resolve them.
o.B: Model the current state of the business using capability, value stream, organization mapping, and information mapping, focus on improving the existing capabilities and value streams because baseline descriptions exist, and document where the business needs to change.
o.C: Review and update the current architecture descriptions to reflect the present state, draw up target descriptions defining new value streams for the delivery business and a capability map for them, map value stream stages to capabilities, and perform a capability gap analysis.
o.D: Request the packaged delivery solution's documentation, define the changes needed to align it with the kitchen and point-of-sale systems, sequence them into an Architecture Roadmap, and get references from other chains to confirm the vendor can meet the dates and service levels.

rat.A: Best (5). Phase B focuses on the business: find where it does not support the change, describe the options and their costs, and work with stakeholders on the trade-offs, engaging them in the decision.
rat.C: Second (3). Updating descriptions and building target value streams and a capability map with a gap analysis is a valid Phase B technique, but it is more model-focused and does not yet require committing to the packaged solution.
rat.B: Third (1). Modeling only, with no stakeholder engagement, and it wrongly assumes the focus should be improving existing capabilities and value streams just because baselines exist.
rat.D: Distractor (0). Not Business Architecture; it is implicit architecture with the architect acting as SME and implementer, jumping to a vendor solution.

questions.stitle: Scenario 3 - Healthcare provider unifying patient portal
questions.scenario: You are a Senior Architect in the EA team of a healthcare provider unifying several patient portals into one experience. The provider uses the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the EA program. A review of the Business Architecture with key stakeholders identified where current value streams and information flows produce inconsistent patient information and slow appointment booking. The stakeholder communities' core motivations were confirmed as faster booking, a consistent patient experience, and driving down the sustained cost of maintaining duplicated portal back-ends. The team leader notes stakeholders agree the experience can improve but the information flows consume heavy IT resources that drive cost up.
questions.q: The team leader asks what you need to establish to address the motivation to drive down sustained cost. Which is the best answer?

o.A: Produce application and data models of the current state, develop a Target Architecture model that enables faster booking and lower cost, create views describing the changes in those terms, and identify the gaps between current and target to build roadmap components.
o.B: Identify where the Application Architecture (the information system services and logical application components) fails to support booking and the patient experience and drives cost up, determine the changes to the information flows that enable faster booking and lower cost, and identify stakeholder priorities for the enhanced capability, improved value stream, and improved information flow.
o.C: Determine where the current Application Architecture and Data Architecture create the information-flow problems, identify the changes needed to fix the flows, look for incremental changes that improve the patient experience, identify the one-time work and its impact on reducing sustainment cost, and check with stakeholders whether the experience improvements are worth the one-time and ongoing cost.
o.D: Determine where the Application and Data Architecture fail to support booking and the patient experience and drive cost up, focus on the logical application and logical data components, identify the changes that improve booking and cost, determine the work, and obtain stakeholder priorities on the application development, data structures, and interfaces.

rat.C: Best (5). All changes carry value and cost; stakeholders accept a Target Architecture on the cost of change and expected outcome, not a data model. Phase C discovers where the current Application and Data Architecture cause the deficiency, then assesses the direct and sustainment cost of the change with stakeholders, feeding Phase E and Phase F.
rat.B: Second (3). It identifies stakeholder priorities and changes to information flows, but does not explicitly assess the one-time and ongoing costs of the change with stakeholders. This leaves cost-of-change information needed by Phases E and F incomplete.
rat.D: Third (1). No analysis of the information flows known to cause the deficiency; it focuses on logical components without a real Target Architecture and asks stakeholders for priorities on implementation detail.
rat.A: Distractor (0). Jumps to modeling and optimizing the Application and Data Architecture with no linkage to the value-stream and information-flow deficiencies from the Business Architecture.

questions.stitle: Scenario 4 - Manufacturer adopting an IoT platform
questions.scenario: You are an Architect in the EA team of an industrial manufacturer deploying a common IoT platform to monitor equipment across its plants. The manufacturer uses the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the EA program. The Business, Data, and Application Architectures are approved by stakeholders and their platform requirements are understood. A Technology Portfolio Catalog and current infrastructure standards exist. Stakeholders are concerned about the resilience of factory-floor connectivity, the security of operational-technology networks, and the cost of scaling the platform across plants. The team leader asks how you would develop the Technology Architecture.

o.A: Document the target platform decomposition in detail, list the technology gaps, and hand them to the infrastructure team to select products, deferring the resilience and cost questions to Implementation Governance.
o.B: Baseline the current technology using the Technology Portfolio Catalog and standards, define the target IoT platform needed to support the approved application and data components, perform a gap analysis against the standards, and work with stakeholders to trade off the resilience, OT-network security, and scaling-cost implications of the candidate technology options.
o.C: Produce a Platform Decomposition Diagram and Environments and Locations Diagram for the target platform, identify the technology gaps against the baseline, record the candidate roadmap components, and refine the diagrams as products are procured.
o.D: Select the IoT platform the largest plant already uses, procure it to accelerate delivery, and document the resulting environment as the Technology Architecture so implementation can start immediately.

rat.B: Best (5). Phase D develops the Technology Architecture that supports the application and data components: baseline with the catalog and standards, define the target, run a gap analysis, and engage stakeholders on the resilience, OT-security, and cost trade-offs they raised. The architect assesses options so stakeholders can decide.
rat.C: Second (3). The platform and environment diagrams plus gap analysis and roadmap components are correct Phase D technique, but they do not surface the resilience, security, and cost trade-offs to stakeholders for decision.
rat.A: Third (1). It produces the target and gaps but hands product selection to the infrastructure team and defers the stakeholders' concerns to a later phase, which is too late.
rat.D: Distractor (0). Jumps to procuring a specific product on plant preference with no Technology Architecture, gap analysis, or trade-off, ignoring the stated concerns.

questions.stitle: Scenario 5 - Retail chain rationalizing supply chain systems
questions.scenario: You are an Enterprise Architect at a retail chain rationalizing fragmented supply-chain systems built up through acquisitions. The chain uses the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the EA program. An Architecture Vision and a set of domain architectures with identified gaps have been approved. The Governing Board requires that peak-season operations continue uninterrupted, that no big-bang cutover occurs, and that each step deliver measurable value. The team has identified the work needed to close the gaps.
questions.q: You have been asked to recommend how to move from the approved gaps to a deliverable plan. Which is the best answer?

o.A: Have each domain architect produce projects that close their own domain's gaps, sum the work per domain into the Implementation and Migration Plan, and record the deliverable timeline in the Architecture Roadmap.
o.B: Implement the domain architectures immediately, revise all in-flight projects to align, expose all data and functionality through defined service interfaces, and publish the result as the Implementation and Migration Plan.
o.C: Ask stakeholders to state what must be done to implement the domain architectures, roll the result into an IT portfolio plan, and produce a comprehensive Target Architecture with detailed technology choices fixed for the next five years.
o.D: Identify the dependencies among the changes and organize them into work packages that address the gaps, assess the value, effort, and risk of each change and work package against stakeholder priorities, define a series of Transition Architectures that each deliver measurable value, and document the work packages and Transition Architectures in the Architecture Roadmap.

rat.D: Best (5). Phase E: identify dependencies, organize changes into work packages, assess value, effort, and risk against stakeholder priorities, and use Transition Architectures to deliver incremental value documented in the Architecture Roadmap, serving the uninterrupted-peak, no-big-bang constraints.
rat.A: Second (3). Names the Plan and Roadmap correctly but rolls up the work domain by domain in an uncoordinated way and does not use Transition Architectures for incremental value.
rat.C: Third (1). Considers stakeholder input but ends in fixed five-year technology choices, negating incremental value and the ability to absorb change.
rat.B: Distractor (0). Jumps to a technical solution (service interfaces), ignores transition and value, and does not follow Phase E guidance.

questions.stitle: Scenario 6 - Merged utilities integrating field operations
questions.scenario: You are Lead Architect at a utility formed by merging a gas and an electricity company. The operating model is unified and an EA project runs as part of the integration. The company uses the TOGAF ADM; the newly appointed CIO sponsors the EA program. An outline Implementation and Migration Plan is approved and detailed planning is under way. Others outside the EA team will fund, build, support, and use what is put in place. The field-operations units have resisted new mobile-workforce processes. The CIO wants risk reduction, timely progress, and an incremental rollout with key value delivered in each increment.
questions.q: You have been asked to describe how the detailed Implementation and Migration Plan should be created. Which is the best answer?

o.A: Have Business Planning, Portfolio Management, and Operations Management join the EA team in migration planning, create detailed resource estimates and business value for all deliverables, plan a series of Transition Architectures that consider stakeholder priorities, finalize the Implementation and Migration Plan, and complete the architecture development cycle once deliverables are done.
o.B: Have the EA team's domain architects define a series of Transition Architectures to deliver value incrementally, create a prioritized activity list documented in the Implementation and Migration Plan with a detailed schedule in the Architecture Roadmap, and circulate these to the field units and Executive Board so they are ready to fund the work.
o.C: Finalize the plan with the domain architects and submit it to the Architecture Board for approval, incorporating its feedback; the plan includes a prioritized project list, approximate cost, estimated effort, schedule, and a sequenced timeline usable as the Architecture Roadmap.
o.D: Have the field Project Managers use the Phase E Implementation and Migration Strategy to build project plans on scope, budget, and time, define business value project by project, select the highest-value projects, and request funding from the Architecture Board.

rat.A: Best (5). Phase F emphasizes collaborative planning with stakeholders inside and outside the organization (Business Planning, Portfolio, Operations Management with the EA team), resource estimates and business value for deliverables, and Transition Architectures based on stakeholder priorities.
rat.B: Second (3). It uses Transition Architectures but is EA-team-centric and merely circulates the result, lacking the close collaborative planning across the wider stakeholder groups.
rat.C: Third (1). Incomplete; it misses the collaborative planning with stakeholders inside and outside the organization that Phase F requires.
rat.D: Distractor (0). Hands strategic migration planning to Project Managers; TOGAF's intent is that the EA gives projects detailed guidance so they focus on operational, not strategic, issues.

questions.stitle: Scenario 7 - Insurer deploying a COTS claims package
questions.scenario: You are Lead Architect at an insurer with a mature EA practice using the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the EA program. After consulting key stakeholders, the CIO has decided to deploy a COTS claims-processing package quickly and within budget. The package requires an application server that is not on the current infrastructure standards list. The Architecture Board noted the non-standard component and the need to protect performance and security KPIs. The CIO has approved the roadmap projects and appointed a project manager, and stresses that performance and security KPIs must be maintained or exceeded and the project must stay within budget.
questions.q: You have been asked to recommend a plan to implement the CIO's direction. Which is the best answer?

o.A: Ask the vendor to modify the application server to meet current standards, build a prototype to explore options, obtain the internal development leads' approval, hand a schedule-focused project plan to the project manager, and review performance after go-live.
o.B: Eliminate the non-standard application server, create a revised plan and Architecture Contract to build a standards-compliant replacement in-house, tell the CIO this is lower cost long term, take the budget impact to the finance committee, and chair frequent project meetings to monitor compliance and schedule.
o.C: Accept the direction, add the application server as an additional organizational standard in the Standards Library (noting the training and skills needed to support it), work with the implementation team to draw up an Architecture Contract, emphasize compliance reviews and performance and security testing during implementation, agree SLAs and dates with the business, and collect reusable artifacts afterward.
o.D: Prepare a detailed risk assessment and impact analysis of the non-standard server, hand the deliverables and deployment dates to the implementation team, obtain CIO approval before implementation starts, test the solution just before deployment to confirm performance, and archive the artifacts in the repository when done.

rat.C: Best (5). All within Phase G: accept the decision already made with stakeholders, add the new standard to the Standards Library (noting training and skills), draw up an Architecture Contract with the implementation team, emphasize compliance reviews and performance and security testing during implementation, agree SLAs and dates with the business, and collect reusable artifacts afterward.
rat.A: Second (3). The vendor change and prototype cost time and budget, which the scenario forbids; the project plan is the project manager's job; and reviewing performance only after go-live is too late.
rat.D: Third (1). Follows the direction but focuses on risk over co-existence, just hands over deliverables and dates with no negotiation on service levels, and tests too late (after the solution is built).
rat.B: Distractor (0). Reverses a decision the CIO already made with stakeholders, makes unsubstantiated cost claims, involves the finance committee irrelevantly, and has the architect chairing project meetings.

questions.stitle: Scenario 8 - Retailer facing a supplier withdrawal
questions.scenario: You are Lead Architect at a retailer whose target architecture is implemented and in production, governed under the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the EA program. A key technology supplier has announced it will withdraw support for a middleware product central to the current architecture within twelve months. A Change Request has been raised describing the resulting deviation. The Architecture Board has asked how to handle it. The change could affect the Application and Technology Architectures and possibly the integration approach across several business systems.
questions.q: You have been asked to recommend how to handle the Change Request. Which is the best answer?

o.A: Log the Change Request in the repository and defer any action until the next scheduled architecture review, since the middleware still has twelve months of support.
o.B: Treat the Change Request as an input to Architecture Change Management, assess its impact through a requirements impact assessment (which requirements, stakeholder priority, which ADM phases to revisit, and recommendations), and on that basis decide whether a simple change update suffices or a new ADM cycle is warranted, referring the recommendation to the Architecture Board and stakeholders.
o.C: Assess the impact of the Change Request across the affected domains and, if the change is contained, apply it as an incremental update to the architecture through change management, escalating to a new ADM cycle only if the impact analysis shows it is warranted.
o.D: Immediately open a new full ADM cycle from the Preliminary Phase to redesign the integration approach, since losing core middleware clearly requires starting over.

rat.B: Best (5). The Change Request is the key input to Phase H. TOGAF requires assessing its impact (requirements affected, stakeholder priority, ADM phases to revisit, recommendations) and then deciding between a change update and a new ADM cycle, with the recommendation going to the board and stakeholders who hold the decision rights.
rat.C: Second (3). It correctly assesses impact and distinguishes an incremental update from a new cycle, but it does not frame the formal requirements impact assessment or the referral of the recommendation to the board and stakeholders.
rat.D: Third (1). Starting a full new cycle may be the outcome, but jumping there without an impact assessment skips the Phase H decision step and may be disproportionate.
rat.A: Distractor (0). Deferring action on a Change Request driven by an imminent support withdrawal ignores the purpose of Phase H, which is to manage change to the architecture as it arises.
